title: The Free Energy Principle & Active Inference: a Systematic Literature Analysis

creators.name: Knight, Virginia Bleu
creators.affiliation: Active Inference Institute, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces NM. Department of Biology

creators.name: Cordes, RJ
creators.affiliation: Cognitive Security and Education Forum (COGSEC), Active Inference Institute

creators.name: Friedman, Daniel
creators.affiliation: Active Inference Institute, Cognitive Security and Education Forum (COGSEC), University of California, Davis. Department of Entomology & Nematology

description: Here we perform a literature analysis of publications in scientific literature using the term “Free Energy Principle” or “Active Inference”, with an emphasis on works written by Karl J Friston. For a subset of papers with accessible full texts, we performed manual annotation (related to structural, visual, and mathematical features) and automated analyses (related to the terms in the Active Inference Institute’s Active Inference Ontology). The initial analysis here, at the scale of thousands of citations and hundreds of annotated papers, is presented as a first step towards the development of systems which could:  Encompass increased scope of relevant works, including non-textual Integrate multiple forms of annotation and participation  Facilitate integration of manual and artificial contributions Feature richer interfaces for use in learning & research Address field-specific local questions and provide transferable approaches Speak to broader questions in the history and philosophy of science  This project is maintained by the Active Inference Institute. This project has an  interactive Coda site  and a Github repository .

methods.name: Publish or Perish / Google Scholar search for FEP, ActInf and Friston papers
methods.description: Citations from 1990–2021 matching the two terms or authored by Karl Friston were collected and de-duplicated manually by title.
methods.evidence: we used Publish or Perish version 8 [16] for the terms “active inference” and/or “free energy principle” as well as papers authored by Karl J. Friston, from 1990 through 2021, searched with Google Scholar.

methods.name: BioPython query of open-access PubMed papers for full-text subset
methods.description: The BioPython API was used to restrict analysis to open-source PubMed papers with the terms in title/abstract.
methods.evidence: we used the BioPython API [17] to query for open source publications with titles and/or abstracts containing the terms “active inference” and/or “free energy principle” listed in the NCBI Pubmed Database

methods.name: PyPDF2 term-frequency extraction using Active Inference Ontology terms
methods.description: A custom PyPDF2 script counted 74 core, 250 supplement and 74 entailed ontology terms in each abstract and PDF.
methods.evidence: The script’s inputs included a list of ontology terms (74 core terms, 250 supplement terms, and 74 entailed terms, archived at [15])

methods.name: Manual annotation of figures, equations, tables, boxes, supplements
methods.description: Each analyzed paper was hand-annotated for structural/mathematical features and estimated citations per year.
methods.evidence: Papers that were analyzed for term usage, were also manually annotated with the following information (Figure 2): # Figures (count of Figures), Figures with equations? (are there equations within Figures), # Equations

methods.name: ResearchRabbit citation network; Coda tables; Orange clustering
methods.description: ResearchRabbit built a citation network of the focal papers; Coda merged data into reflexive tables; Orange clustered term usage.
methods.evidence: Research Rabbit [20] was used to analyze citations and construct an co-citation network of the focal set of papers (where nodes represent publications, and edges reflect an instance of one paper citing another).

key_findings: From the larger FEP/ActInf citation corpus, the analysis focused on an initial set of 237 open-access papers obtained via PubMed.
The most highly cited papers in the open-source dataset were from 2013 and all included Karl J. Friston as an author.
By citations per year, Friston is not in the top five first authors; Sterzer (109.3) and Carhart-Harris (108.5) lead, and top papers by this metric date from 2018–2020.
All core Active Inference Ontology terms increased in use frequency over time.
Term frequencies tracked specific publications, e.g. 'Information Geometry' rose after Parr et al. 2019 and 'Cognitivism' after Friston & Allen 2018.
key_findings_evidence: From the large corpus of FEP/ActInf citations, we focused our analysis on an initial set of 237 papers via PubMed.
Figure 4 demonstrates that the most highly cited publications in our open source dataset were from 2013, and all included Karl J. Friston as an author.

The top five first authors with the highest average citations per year are, in order: Phillip Sterzer (109.3), R.L. Carhart-Harris (108.5), Michael Kirchoff (89), Giovanni Pezzulo (71.5), and Maxwell Ramstead (58.2).
Figure 9A illustrates that all core ontology terms (see Coda site and [22]) increased in use frequency over time.

Here it can be seen that the frequency of the term Information Geometry increased following the publication by Parr et al., 2019 which focused on the significance of the information geometry of the Markov blanket.

summary_provenance.method: Evidence-grounded extraction from full_text.md: every method and finding carries a verbatim quote from the paper text, mechanically verified to occur in full_text.md (whitespace/ligature-normalized) before merge.
summary_provenance.notes: No quantitative analysis was performed on the citation network; authors flag PDF-extraction and nested-term counting limitations.
